sounds.intro: Greek has its own alphabet with 24 letters. The Latin shown is written by rule from the Greek, the way the word sounds. Every noun is masculine, feminine or neuter. A stress mark (ά) shows which syllable is loud, and the capitals in the say line show it too.
rows: a soft gargle before a, o, u; like "y" before e or i
"b" and "d" at the start of a word; "mb" and "nd" inside
notes: Greek has two e-sounds in writing (ε, αι) and several ee-sounds (η, ι, ει, οι, υ). You will have to learn the spelling word by word.
The Latin line is written by rule from the Greek. Where the Latin looks odd, trust the Greek and the say line.

grammar.title: Pronouns
text: Greek often drops the pronoun, because the verb ending shows who is speaking. "Αυτός" is he, "αυτή" is she and "αυτό" is it.
ex: afti ine i megali adelfi mou
af-TEE EE-neh ee meh-GHAH-lee ah-thel-FEE moo
αυτή είναι η μεγάλη αδελφή μου

grammar.title: Singular and plural
text: Nouns have three genders: ο (masculine), η (feminine), το (neuter). The plural article is οι for masculine and feminine, and τα for neuter. The ending changes: ο μαθητής, οι μαθητές.

grammar.title: To be: είμαι, είσαι, είναι
text: "To be" is a real verb. The pronoun is usually dropped.

grammar.title: Έχω: have
text: "Έχω" means "I have". It is also used for "there is": υπάρχει.

grammar.title: Present tense
text: The verb ending shows the person. Γράφω (to write): γράφω, γράφεις, γράφει, γράφουμε, γράφετε, γράφουν.

grammar.title: Basic sentences
text: The usual order is who, verb, what, but Greek is flexible. Use the article: ο, η, το.

grammar.title: Negation
text: Put "δεν" before the verb: γράφω (I write), δεν γράφω (I do not write).
ex: I do not have a car
he does not work on Sundays

grammar.title: Asking questions
text: The word order does not change. Just raise your voice at the end. In writing, the question mark looks like a semicolon.

grammar.title: Question words
text: Question words stand at the start of the sentence.

grammar.title: Possessives and liking
text: Put the short word after the noun: μου (my), σου (your), του / της (his / her), μας (our), σας (your, formal), τους (their). To like something, say "it pleases me": μου αρέσει.

grammar.title: Formal vs informal
text: εσύ (informal): friends, family, children. εσείς (formal): strangers, older people, work. The verb ending changes: -εις (informal), -ετε (formal).
rows: to onoma sou / to onoma sas
το όνομά σου / το όνομά σας

grammar.title: Past and future (simple)
text: The past changes the stem and adds an ending: πήγα (I went). The future is "θα" + the verb: θα πάω (I will go).

grammar.title: Commands
text: Informal: one form (έλα). Formal and plural: add -τε (ελάτε). To forbid, use "μην" before the verb.

grammar.title: Can, must, want
text: Can: μπορώ να + verb. Must: πρέπει να + verb. Want: θέλω να + verb.
ex: I do not want to eat

grammar.title: In, on, at
text: "Σε" means in, on or at. It joins with the article: σε + το = στο, σε + την = στην. Other words: από (from), για (for), με (with).
ex: the book is on the table
the cat is under the table

grammar.title: Comparing things
text: Put "πιο" before the adjective for "more": πιο μεγάλος. For "the most" add the article: ο πιο μεγάλος. "Than" is "από".
